text: hundred. Classrooms had multiplied, doors appearing in walls that hadn't had them before, the whole structure spreading outward and inward simultaneously like something organic. The Entity had renovated thoroughly and without apology, and the result was something that had stopped pretending to make sense. Shadows clung too tight in the corners. The walls didn’t meet right. The beam from the flashlight couldn’t quite seem to settle anywhere useful, making everything feel ever so slightly like a fever dream. Orela had apparently been with the rest of the survivors, only venturing out when the group had heard the boys make their miraculous resurgence into the land of the semi-dry, nearly walking straight into the hole they had just escaped from in the process. Limping into the classroom, the boys found Leon and Jake waiting in the dark, looking confused and more than a little surprised in the thin flashlight beam. David slumped heavily into the chair at the teacher’s desk, arms braced, eyes locked on a far point in the floor that he wasn’t really seeing. Water still clung to him in rivulets, pooling at his feet as his clothes dripped a slow, steady rhythm. Orela crouched beside him, flashlight angled low as she tried gauging his pupils without blinding him further. "You’re gonna crash," she murmured. "Your system’s still in full burn. You need to rest." "Not yet," David muttered, not looking at her. "Don’t have time. I'll be fine." He wasn't fine. She could see that easily enough — the way he held his shoulder slightly wrong, the controlled quality of his breathing that meant he was managing something he wasn't acknowledging. He'd been in the water long enough and worked hard enough that the consequences were coming whether he cooperated or not. He knew it too. That was the problem. His heart was still hammering like it hadn’t realized the danger was over. His lungs ached, raw and tight. The skin over his back twitched with ghost-water, nerves refusing to settle. He could still feel the moment Dwight found him, how everything slowed, muffled, his thoughts collapsing inward. There hadn’t been enough air in the world. He refused to feel that again. But beneath the desk, his legs betrayed him, shaking faintly, despite how still he sat. His shoulder throbbed. Probably from ramming it into that desk in the stairwell. Or maybe from hauling Dwight by the arm like a sack of potatoes through a hallway that shouldn’t have existed. His spine pulsed with delayed adrenaline. Every second he didn’t move, he was losing ground. If he stopped pushing, stopped performing functional — the thing he'd been holding at arm's length since they'd clawed out of that hole was going to catch up with him. If he fell, he wasn’t sure he’d get back up. Orela sighed, casting the beam toward the door. The hallway stretched beyond it in flickering shadow, and for now, nothing stirred. Leon lingered near the door, glancing down the corridor with one hand on his empty holster. His shoulders twitched. There was a tightness in his movements — familiar tension, the darkness having set off a well worn in paranoia he couldn’t shake. Dwight had folded himself onto one of the low children's desks, shoulders slumped from the weight of the ordeal. His clothes were soaked, his face drawn. The adrenaline was draining fast, leaving him hollow and shaking. He looked vacant, but his hands gripped the edge of the desk tight, feet planted firm on the ground as if trying to anchor himself. He wasn't shaking anymore, not visibly, but the stillness had a quality to it that wasn't calm. His eyes tracked the room without settling on anything. Jake was perched on the counter, slamming the straight end of a half-rusted crowbar against the window. The glass refused to shatter, absorbing each strike with a soundless thud. He cursed under his breath and gave it a final smack before hopping off the counter. "This is insane. It's not even tempered glass. What the hell is this place MADE of?" David turned his head to face him. “How long have you three been up here, anyways?” “Been in here half an hour, maybe more,” Jake said, prying at the frame. “Thought it was just us and Orela. Doors started showing up everywhere and closed up behind us. Like the building didn’t want anyone else in. Feels like the place has doubled in size since we got in” Orela nodded in agreement, gesturing around the classroom with the flashlight. “Classrooms repeat. Some of them shift. I chalked it up to the usual Entity bullshit, but...” Dwight lifted his head slightly. “You guys got doors, we had faulty plumbing. Pipes were bursting. Something’s wrong with the space.” Leon’s brow furrowed. “Like... what?” “Distances felt off. Sounds vanished. Water rose faster than it should’ve. Way faster.” He swallowed. “It wasn’t just leaking. It was... flooding. Like it was pushing it through the floor. Way more than broken pipes should have had.” He kept his voice even and mostly managed it, though his hands tightened on the edge of the desk while he talked. "How fast?" Dwight hesitated. “Up to our ribs in minutes.” David grunted. “Hit the ceiling before we made it halfway down the connecting hallway.” He spared a glance at Dwight, who had gone back to curling against himself, voice soft. “It was so disorienting. Nothing was where it should have been. We lost my flashlight at some point... I had to go back to drag David out.” Leon nodded once, his hand clenched at his side, reflexive. A muscle twitched in his jaw. He looked down at the floor — to the thin spread of water that Dwight and David had tracked in with them, pooling dark against the tile — and he took one step to the side, away from the puddle he'd been standing in, without appearing to notice he'd done it.
